meta.name: Irish Setter First Year Costs
meta.excerpt: Irish Setter ownership costs $4,800–$9,250 in the first year. Large-breed food costs and pet insurance are the major ongoing expenses after purchase.

intro.label: What You'll Spend
intro.heading: Irish Setter First-Year Cost Breakdown
intro.html:
An Irish Setter is not a cheap dog to bring home, and it isn't meant to be. Responsible breeding for this breed means CLAD and PRA DNA testing on both parents — screening that eliminates a fatal immune disorder and a blinding eye disease before a puppy is ever born. That testing, plus the breed's popularity and the slow, careful way good Irish Setter breeders raise litters, keeps purchase prices in the $3,000–$6,000 range. Everything after that purchase price is fairly ordinary large-breed upkeep: food for a 60–70 lb dog, routine veterinary care, and insurance sized to a breed with a couple of known hereditary risks.

ExpenseFirst YearAnnual (ongoing)
Puppy (CLAD- and PRA-tested breeder)$3,000–$6,000—
Food (large, active breed)$500–$800$500–$800
Vet (routine + puppy series)$500–$900$350–$600
Pet insurance$500–$1,000$500–$1,000
Setup (large crate, feathering-safe grooming tools, supplies)$300–$550—
Estimated Total$4,800–$9,250$1,350–$2,400

Why the price spread is so wide

The $4,800 end of that range assumes a puppy at the lower end of breeder pricing, a modest insurance plan, and no unplanned vet visits. The $9,250 end assumes a puppy from a well-known field or show line, a comprehensive insurance policy, and the kind of first-year puppy incident (an ear infection from those long drop ears, a bout of GI upset from counter-surfing) that's extremely common in a breed this food-motivated and physically clumsy. Because Irish Setters are field-bred sporting dogs with genuine working drive, many puppies also come from breeders who require a signed contract about exercise, structured activity, and sometimes even a spay/neuter timeline tied to hip and eye clearances — none of which changes the sticker price, but all of which reflects the seriousness with which this breed is bred.

care.label: Biggest Costs
care.heading: Key Cost Considerations
care.html:
Gastropexy: a small upfront cost against a catastrophic one

Irish Setters carry a deep, narrow chest — the classic conformation associated with bloat and GDV (gastric dilatation-volvulus). A prophylactic gastropexy performed at the same time as spay or neuter tacks $200–$500 onto that surgery. In exchange, it surgically tacks the stomach in place so it cannot twist, which is the part of bloat that actually kills dogs. Emergency GDV surgery without a prior gastropexy runs $3,000–$8,000, requires overnight hospitalization, and still carries real mortality risk even with prompt treatment. For an active, deep-chested breed that eats fast and exercises hard, this is one of the clearest cost-benefit decisions in dog ownership — bring it up at the very first vet visit, before the spay/neuter is even scheduled.

Hip Dysplasia

Hip dysplasia shows up in Irish Setters as it does in most large, fast-growing sporting breeds, and its cost depends entirely on severity. Medical management — weight control, joint supplements, NSAIDs during flare-ups, occasional rehab sessions — runs $500–$1,500 annually in moderate cases. A dog that needs surgical correction faces $3,500–$7,000 per hip. Enrolling in pet insurance before the first vet visit, ideally as a puppy with no pre-existing findings on record, is the single biggest lever an owner has over whether this becomes a covered expense or an out-of-pocket one.

CLAD and PRA: costs you pay before you own the dog

Unlike hip dysplasia or bloat, Canine Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency (CLAD) and progressive retinal atrophy (PRA) are costs the breeder absorbs, not the owner — but they matter enormously to the purchase decision. CLAD is fatal; affected puppies cannot fight routine infection and typically die in puppyhood. It's a simple recessive gene, and DNA testing both parents before breeding guarantees no affected puppies result. PRA testing similarly protects against a slow, progressive blindness that has no treatment. When you're comparing two Irish Setter litters at similar prices, ask directly to see both parents' CLAD and PRA clearances — a breeder who can't produce them is not a breeder worth the $3,000+ price tag, regardless of how the puppies look.

Ears and the feathered coat

The Irish Setter's long, low-set, heavily feathered ears trap moisture and restrict airflow, which makes ear infections a recurring, budget-relevant issue rather than a rare event. A basic ear cleaning solution costs under $15 and, used weekly as part of the grooming routine, prevents most infections. Left unmanaged, an infected ear means a vet visit ($75–$150) plus medicated drops ($20–$50) — a cost that's almost entirely avoidable with a few minutes of weekly maintenance. The silky feathering on the legs, tail, chest, and ears itself needs brushing two to three times a week to prevent mats from forming behind the ears, in the armpits, and around the britches — areas owners commonly neglect until a mat requires shaving out.

special.label: Lifetime Budget
special.heading: Lifetime Cost Estimate
special.html:
At 12–15 years, Irish Setters live longer than many large breeds, which stretches the lifetime total but also means the annual average cost is spread over more years of companionship.

ScenarioEstimated Lifetime Cost
Healthy dog, no surgical hip or GDV events$25,000–$45,000
Hip dysplasia requiring surgery$35,000–$60,000

A Month-by-Month Look at Year One

Costs don't land evenly across the first twelve months — they front-load hard, then flatten out.

Months 1–3: the setup crunch

This is when the puppy price, a large-breed crate sized for a 60–70 lb adult (buy the adult size with a divider panel rather than replacing it three times as your setter grows), the first round of puppy vaccines, deworming, microchipping, and initial grooming tools all land at once. Expect this window alone to account for $4,000–$7,500 of the first-year total, most of it the puppy price itself plus the one-time gear.

Months 4–6: vaccines finish, training starts, energy explodes

The final vaccine boosters and the spay/neuter (ideally with that prophylactic gastropexy discussed above) happen in this window, typically $400–$700 combined. This is also when an Irish Setter puppy's energy genuinely outpaces a casual owner's expectations — a 20-minute walk stops being enough somewhere around month four, and group puppy class ($100–$200 for six weeks) becomes less optional and more essential for teaching recall before the dog is fast enough that recall failures become dangerous.

Months 7–12: steady state arrives

By month seven, the one-time costs are behind you. What remains is food, routine preventives, and whatever insurance premium you've chosen. Most households see monthly spend settle to roughly $150–$250 during this stretch, with the wide range depending mostly on the insurance tier chosen and whether the puppy transitions cleanly to adult food or needs a formula change along the way.

Food Math for a 60–70 Pound Adult

An adult Irish Setter at the breed's typical 60–70 lb weight eats roughly 3–4 cups of a quality large-breed kibble per day, split across two meals. A 30-pound bag of a mid-to-premium formula runs roughly $50–$70 and, at that intake, lasts about 4–5 weeks for an adult — landing squarely inside the $500–$800 annual figure above. Puppies eat a large-breed puppy formula on a different feeding schedule (three meals a day, tapering to two), and the transition to adult food typically happens between 12 and 18 months, later than smaller breeds, because large-breed puppy formulas are specifically calibrated to slow growth and protect developing joints — an important detail given this breed's hip dysplasia risk. Skipping the large-breed puppy formula to save a few dollars a bag is a false economy here; it directly works against joint health you're otherwise paying to protect.

Grooming: DIY Kit vs. Professional Schedule

The Irish Setter's silky, feathered coat is genuinely lower-maintenance than a curly or double coat in terms of shedding, but the feathering itself needs consistent attention or it mats. A DIY kit — a slicker brush, a metal comb for the feathering, ear cleaner, and nail clippers — costs $60–$100 one time and, with weekly at-home brushing, is sufficient for most owners who stay consistent. Owners who prefer a professional groomer for bathing, sanitary trims, and feathering maintenance typically pay $50–$80 per visit every 6–8 weeks, or roughly $300–$650 annually — worth budgeting separately from the food and vet lines above if you know you won't keep up with brushing yourself.

Two Realistic First-Year Paths

ItemBudget PathPremium Path
Puppy or adoption$3,000 (breeder) or $250–$600 (rescue)$6,000 (established field/show line)
Food$500$800
Vet + gastropexy add-on$500$900 + $500
Insurance$500$1,000 (comprehensive)
Setup + grooming tools$300$550 + $650 professional grooming
Approximate Total$4,800 (breeder) / $2,050 (rescue)$9,400

One-Time vs. Recurring Costs

  • One-time only: puppy price or adoption fee, crate and initial supplies, spay/neuter with optional gastropexy, initial vaccine series, microchip, DIY grooming kit.
  • Recurring every year: food, insurance premium, annual exam and boosters, flea/heartworm prevention, ear-care supplies, professional grooming (if chosen), training refreshers.

Smart Ways to Save — and Traps to Avoid — With This Breed

  1. Adopt through Irish Setter Rescue. Adult adoption fees run $250–$600 versus $3,000–$6,000 for a puppy, and adopted adults are often already spayed/neutered, vaccinated, and past the destructive chewing phase — genuinely lower risk, not just lower cost.
  2. Don't skip the gastropexy to save $200–$500. Given this breed's deep chest, this is the one place where cutting the upfront cost sets up a dramatically larger emergency bill later.
  3. Buy the adult-sized crate up front with a divider. A 60–70 lb dog needs a large crate eventually; buying small and upgrading twice costs more overall than one large crate with a movable panel.
  4. Do weekly ear cleaning and feathering brushing yourself. A $60–$100 DIY kit prevents both the matted-coat shave-down and the recurring ear infection vet visits that quietly add up over a year.
  5. Get insurance quotes before month one is over. Because hip dysplasia and GDV are both known risks in this breed, enrolling before any symptom appears in the medical record is the difference between a covered condition and an excluded one.

A false economy specific to this breed: buying a cheap puppy from an unverified source to avoid the $3,000+ price floor. Without CLAD testing, you're gambling on a fatal, incurable condition; without PRA testing, you risk a dog that goes blind in early middle age. The savings on the puppy price disappear instantly against either outcome, financially and otherwise.

Regional Cost Variation

Urban markets on the coasts push vet visits, boarding, and professional grooming 20–40 percent above the national averages used here — a routine exam that's $75 in a small Midwestern town can be $110–$140 in a major metro. Insurance premiums follow similar geography since they're partly priced on local vet costs. Suburban and rural households, which also happen to suit this breed's exercise needs far better than a small city apartment, tend to see the lower end of every range in the tables above.

Years Two Through Twelve: The Long Middle

After the puppy year, costs drop meaningfully — no more acquisition cost, no more initial vaccine series, no more one-time gear. The middle years of an Irish Setter's life, roughly ages 2 through 7, tend to be the cheapest medically, with annual ongoing costs in the $1,350–$2,400 range shown in the first table holding fairly steady. Insurance premiums tend to creep upward a few percent per year and jump more noticeably once the dog is reclassified as a senior around age 7–8. Food costs stay roughly flat since adult formula pricing tracks close to puppy formula pricing. What changes most is vigilance: senior bloodwork, dental cleanings, and monitoring for hip or joint changes become the new routine cost drivers as the dog moves into its senior years.

faq.q: Why does breeder CLAD and PRA testing matter so much for the purchase price?
faq.a: CLAD (Canine Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency) is fatal — affected puppies can't fight off ordinary infections and typically die young — and PRA causes incurable progressive blindness. Both are simple recessive genes, meaning DNA-testing both parents before breeding guarantees no affected puppies. That testing costs the breeder relatively little against the $3,000–$6,000 puppy price, so any Irish Setter breeder who can't produce both clearances on paper isn't one worth buying from, regardless of how appealing the price looks.

faq.q: Is a prophylactic gastropexy really necessary for this breed?
faq.a: Given the Irish Setter's deep, narrow chest, yes — it's one of the clearest cost decisions in the breed. Adding gastropexy to a spay/neuter costs $200–$500 and permanently removes the twisting (volvulus) component of bloat. Skip it, and an emergency GDV surgery later costs $3,000–$8,000 with a real risk the dog doesn't survive even with prompt treatment. Ask your vet about it at the very first appointment, well before scheduling the spay/neuter.

faq.q: Is pet insurance worth carrying on an Irish Setter?
faq.a: Generally yes, and earlier is better. Because hip dysplasia and GDV are both documented breed risks, enrolling as a puppy — before either condition has any chance to appear in the medical record — is what keeps them covered rather than excluded as pre-existing. Insurance is best thought of as protection against the one catastrophic bill, not a way to offset routine costs like food or annual exams. Read the hereditary-condition exclusions carefully before choosing a policy.

faq.q: Which years of Irish Setter ownership are cheapest?
faq.a: Roughly ages 2 through 7. By then the puppy price, initial vaccine series, spay/neuter, and setup gear are all behind you, and age-related conditions haven't set in yet. Expect annual ongoing costs in the $1,350–$2,400 range during this stretch — mostly food, prevention, and whatever insurance tier you've chosen — before senior care costs start climbing again around age 7–8.

faq.q: How big an emergency fund should I keep for an Irish Setter specifically?
faq.a: Aim for $1,500–$3,000 set aside, on top of insurance. This breed's two headline risks — GDV and hip dysplasia — both often require an upfront deposit before a clinic will operate, even with insurance in place, since most policies reimburse after the fact rather than paying the vet directly. The emergency fund covers that gap and the deductible; insurance covers the rest of a large surgical bill.

faq.q: Can someone on a tighter budget realistically own an Irish Setter?
faq.a: It's possible but requires honesty about the breed's real costs, both financial and time-related. Outside one-time annual expenses, ongoing monthly spend (food, prevention, insurance, incidentals) for a 60–70 lb dog runs roughly $110–$200, and this is not a breed that tolerates a minimal-exercise lifestyle regardless of budget. Adopting an adult through Irish Setter Rescue lowers the acquisition cost substantially and skips the puppy-stage expenses, which can make the breed workable on a tighter budget than buying a puppy would.

faq.q: Why is the first year so much pricier than every year after it?
faq.a: Almost the entire gap comes down to costs that happen exactly once: the puppy price itself, the full initial vaccine series, spay/neuter (plus the gastropexy add-on worth doing on this breed), microchipping, and the crate and gear a new puppy needs on day one. All of that lands inside the first three to six months. From year two onward, none of it repeats, and the budget narrows down to food, prevention, and insurance — which is why the ongoing annual figure is roughly a quarter of the first-year total.
